I was struggling with this on Godot on iPad this week.  More than once I thought it was a deadlock, and spent hours chasing it, assuming it was specific to me.  But this is the same stack trace.

In the end, I am not sure if it is fixed, but using Stuart’s lazy loading + my own pre baked shaders made the issue go away for me.  It happened on the museum app.

At this point, I like to believe that the issue is that a massive slowdown caused by shader compilation (I shared some stats a few messages ago) and not a real dead lock.  But I could be wrong.

It would help to see all the stack traces for all the threads (on iOS, while I could get all these stack traces, I could never spot the one doing the actual compilation - this is the sole thing that makes me think i have masked rather than fixed the problem).  I even instrumented MutexLock to track it, so I think the issue is fixed, but getting the stack trace on other platforms might help confirm if this is deadlock or just the system overwhelmed with shaders than need compiling

Sorry the stats were shared on the chat group.

Launching the Museum sample creates over 3,600 shaders.  Even on my M2 Ultra compiling took several minutes, it took so long to batch compile that I went to lunch and I didn’t measure the time.  

It produced about 100 megs worth of metal shader code in 20 million lines of code.

Only a fraction of the shaders are used, which is why Stuart’s patch for lazy loading on Mac helps so much.  But I am little troubled that I still have to keep 100 megs worth of text in ram.

> Only a fraction of the shaders are used, which is why Stuart’s patch for lazy loading on Mac helps so much. But I am little troubled that I still have to keep 100 megs worth of text in ram.

Godot's approach since 4.0 is to precompile as many shaders as possible on startup, as we don't know in advance which features the project will use. This could be improved by https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/102552 though, since it could also gather a list of features in the project that may be used at some point in the project. (It would also need to look through scripts to check for toggleable options though.)

Additionally, the project settings added by https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/5229 could be used to avoid compiling shaders for disabled features. This means you'd get a stutter the first time you enable the feature from the project settings or RenderingServer method, but it's probably acceptable if this happens while in a settings menu, as opposed to during gameplay.

I'm still surprised to see 3,600 unique shaders being compiled in MOAT though. Even with all features enabled in a 3D project with a few dozen materials, I'd expect the number to be a quarter of that at most. There's a chance that project may be using Shader resources in other resources that are marked **Local to Scene**, which will trigger a shader compilation for every instance.

Nice stacktrace! We can clearly see here the presence of a deadlock.

1. We have WorkerThreadPool tasks calling `SceneShaderForwardClustered::_create_shader_func()` which waits on `singleton_lock.
2. Then in the another WorkerThreadPool task, there is the `SceneShaderForwardClustered::ShaderData::is_valid()` function which holds a `singleton_lock` for the entirety of `ShaderRD::version_is_valid(version)`.
3. `version_is_valid()` calls `_compile_ensure_finished` which calls `_compile_version_end`, which waits for task group completion **while still holding `singleton_lock`**, on the very tasks that are waiting for `singleton_lock`. This is a deadlock.

So what can we fix here? We need to somehow ensure that the `singleton_lock` is not being held at the time that `wait_for_group_task_completion` is invoked, while also ensuring that you don't get multiple threads trampling all over the state of `ShaderRD`. It doesn't look simple to fix, but this issue seems quite severe.

I'm adding the crash label since a deadlock is effectively a crash and I can't find a better label for deadlock.

Edit: One workaround could be to force shader compilation onto a single-threaded WorkerThreadPool, so that it will still get the task dependency calculations but without any risk of deadlock (though I wonder if you'd be hitting lock reentrancy and if there could still be state corruption caused by reentrant locking, given that the code did not seem to consider this).

Based on @stuartcarnie great analysis of the deadlock here: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/102812 this happens to be a very common problem with thread pool deadlocks.   

There are no great general purpose solutions to this problem, but here are some of the band-aids that are used in Java and .NET to solve this very common problem:

1. Have a "growing" thread pool that adds threads with some cadence (like spawn a new thread for the thread pool every second or so if you are under duress).   But you also need to implement pool shrinkage.
2. Use separate thread pool for these tasks - use a dedicated thread pool for say the shader compilers, independent of the pool used for other tasks.

None trivial or pleasant to write - and worst of all, they are just band-aids for the underlying design problem.   So I would not even try to attempt those.

But I think there is an even better option for Godot, which would be: set an upper limit to how many threads can be used for shader compilation at once - manually enforcing that there is room left on the thread pool to ensure forward progress.

The idea would be to modify `ShaderRD::_compile_version_start` to check how many tasks it has enqueued on the WorkerThreadPool and anything about a certain threshold, would get added to a queue, rather than immediately placed on the WorkerThreadPool - and the `_compile_version_end` would need to drain that queue as it makes progress.

> Use separate thread pool for these tasks - use a dedicated thread pool for say the shader compilers, independent of the pool used for other tasks.

Yeah, this approach sadly mostly kicks the can down the road.   The long-term solution in Java was the introduction of virtual threads (effectively, infinite and cheap threads).  A peer of problems also appeared on the Apple platform, with `libdispatch`, so Apple's solution was a pretty strict rule in Swift: tasks should always make forward progress, to the point where using locks in tasks is not possible in the language.

So I think that the best approach is to place a queuing system in front of the WorkerThreadPool, which is both cheaper than the heavy duty real Java/Swift solutions, is not a workaround and has the advantage of being correct (within the confines of still needing a heuristic for "How many threads should we allocate"?)
